title: love as a method
hook: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water: what the Gita says is enough

segments.voice: Yesterday, seva, and Hanuman with a mountain in his hands. Your line was do something for someone, quietly. If you did it, did some part of you want to tell somebody? Day sixteen.

A leaf. A flower. A piece of fruit. A little water. That list came up on day eight, at the home shrine, and back then the point was how small the gifts are. Today, read the rest of the sentence. In the ninth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says that whoever offers him one of these with love, he accepts it, because it was offered with love. The gift isn't what makes it count. The love is. And the Sanskrit word for that love sits right inside the verse. A whole way of walking this path is built on it, a way full of songs, drums, bells and late nights of singing. It's today's word.
screen: `A LEAF, A FLOWER, AGAIN.` → `OFFERED WITH LOVE.` → `THE WORD INSIDE THE VERSE.`

segments.voice: Bhakti. Devotion. Love turned toward God and practiced on purpose, the way you'd practice an instrument. You've spent some of this camp with the head: atman, Brahman, the self and the whole. Bhakti is the heart, and the Gita treats it as a full path of its own. In the Gita's telling, nobody has to master the ideas first. The way in is love. Devotees aim that love at God in different forms, Krishna, Rama, Shiva, the Goddess, and the move is the same. Tradition remembers a woman who showed it. Mirabai was a princess in what is now Rajasthan, and the stories say that from childhood she thought of Krishna as her own. Married into a royal family, she kept singing to him in the temple, in public, with ordinary devotees. Her in-laws, the stories go, were furious. They sent her poison, and it did her no harm. Whatever you make of those details, her songs are still sung. Here's why bhakti is a method and not only a mood. Moods come and go. The lamp gets lit anyway. The song gets sung on the tired night too. Some who practice it say the feeling catches up with the doing, not the other way around. Go back to the leaf: what the verse looks for is the love it's offered with, and love, on this path, is something you keep doing. That's part of why this path can be so loud. Bells, drums, a crowd singing the same name over and over. That's bhakti with the volume up.
screen: `BHAKTI — LOVE, PRACTICED ON PURPOSE.` · `THE HEART IS A PATH TOO.` · `MIRABAI KEPT SINGING.` · `THE LAMP GETS LIT ANYWAY.` · then, large: `DEVOTION IS A VERB.`

segments.voice: The practice today: offer a leaf. Find one small thing within reach. A sip of water, a flower, a breath, even just your open hand. Hold it for a moment. If you pray, you can offer it, with love, to God in whatever form you know. If you don't, offer it to whatever you love most in the world, and let the feeling be as big as it wants to be. Nobody's watching. The bell holds the time.
Bhakti. Devotion. Love you practice, not only love you feel. A leaf, offered whole. Sixteenth word.
Your line: devotion is a verb. Today, do one loving thing on a day you don't feel like it. That's the method, all of it. Day sixteen.

screen: `DAY 16 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE COURAGE NOT TO STRIKE.`

howItsDone: Bhakti shapes Hindu worship in temples and homes: devotees sing bhajans and kirtan, offer flowers, fruit and water at home shrines and temples, and repeat the names of God, often together and out loud.

original.note: Sanskrit: devotion, loving attention to God.

trapdoor: what you thought: bhakti is a feeling of being very religious.
what it means: love turned toward God and practiced, like an instrument. a leaf offered with love is enough.
what a scholar hears: Bhagavad Gita 9.26, the leaf, flower, fruit and water, and the Gita's long teaching on devotion as its own path.

notes: Gita 9.26 paraphrased (patram pushpam phalam toyam). Arnold 1885 has a rendering; not quoted because exact wording unverified. Confirm the paraphrase and 'ninth chapter'.

Mirabai: the princess, marriage into a royal (Mewar) family, singing with devotees in temples and the poison story are given as 'the stories say'; manuscript's 'sixteenth century', 'hundreds of songs', 'five hundred years' and 'one of the most loved figures' cut under the claims rule. Confirm framing.
'People who practice it often say the feeling catches up with the doing' is a general observation, softened from the manuscript; confirm.
Forms named (Krishna, Rama, Shiva, the Goddess) without ranking; confirm the list suits the path.

Editor pass: day 8 (puja) already taught Gita 9.26 as 'the size of the offering was never the point', with a matching myth item; the hook, teach line, match pair and myth item now take a new angle (the word bhakti inside the verse: bhaktya, bhakty-upahritam) instead of repeating it. 'Often say' softened to 'some say'; 'Rajasthan' made 'what is now Rajasthan'.

Audit (2026-10-01): 'You don't have to master the ideas first. You have to love.' told the listener what they must do; now attributed to the Gita ('in the Gita's telling... the way in is love'), with the myth reveal matched. Mirabai is usually placed at Merta, married into the Mewar (Sisodia) house; 'princess' is the common telling. No other errors found.
Editor review 2: 'that's why this path can be so loud' was an unsourced causal claim, softened to 'part of why'; practice opener varied.
